tagline.text: A waterfall dropping into a jungle canyon at the bottom of 335 steps

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱600–1,800 per person (day trip from Dumaguete)

image.credit: Alexey Prokhorov / CC BY 3.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A slender waterfall dropping about 30m into a narrow canyon on the slopes of Mount Talinis, a 30–40 minute drive from Dumaguete. Reaching it means descending roughly 335 steps and crossing a rocky streambed, giving visitors a genuine taste of jungle trekking in a short outing.
Casaroro Falls is hidden deep in a mountain gorge in Barangay Apolong, Valencia, in southeastern Negros Island, in Negros Oriental Province. It lies only about
13km
from downtown Dumaguete, a mere
30–40 minutes
by car, yet the moment you reach the entrance, a completely different world of dense tropical rainforest opens up. The water drops in a single straight column about
(100 feet) high through a sheer rock wall, thin and long like a horse's tail, making it one of the most photographed waterfalls in Negros Oriental.
The water comes from springs high on Mount Talinis (also called Cuernos de Negros), which rises to about

above sea level. Because the area is volcanic terrain, the canyon floor is strewn with large, rounded boulders coated in moss and ferns, keeping the air damp and cool. From the entrance you descend roughly 335 concrete steps, then walk about
20–30 minutes
over the streambed's rocks and across the stream two or three times before the falls finally come into view.

Casaroro has repeatedly lost its access path to typhoons and heavy rain over the years. When rising floodwater sweeps away bridges and walkways, temporary bamboo or log bridges go up, and the steps and railings get repaired again and again. Trail conditions can therefore vary quite a bit depending on when you visit — but that same cycle has also kept the site from being heavily developed, leaving it with a raw, unpolished feel.

It's an easy half-day outing for travelers based in Dumaguete, and it pairs well with nearby Pulangbato Falls, Red Rock hot spring, and Twin Lakes for a full day exploring the Valencia highlands. Families with children can manage the trek if they have the stamina for the stairs, but the climb back up can be tough for anyone with weak knees or older travelers.
Past the entrance restaurant and ticket booth, an endless concrete staircase begins its descent into the canyon. Going down takes only
10–15 minutes
, but hold the railing and watch your footing as you go. The canyon views glimpsed through the trees along the way are refreshing.

Once the stairs end, you follow a boulder-strewn streambed upriver toward the falls. Depending on the water level, you'll cross the stream two or three times on bamboo bridges or stepping stones — on some days the water reaches your knees, making this stretch both the fun and the challenge of the Casaroro trek.

blocks.title: Standing Before the 30m Column of Water

children.text: At the end of the deep canyon, a single column of water drops straight down between rock walls — a scene far more impressive in person than in photos. The roar, the spray, and the cool air arrive all at once, instantly rewarding the effort of the descent.

blocks.title: Swimming in the Cold Falls Pool

children.text: During the dry season, when the flow is moderate, you can swim in the green pool beneath the falls. The water, coming straight down from the mountain, stays quite cold even in peak summer. If the current is strong or the water looks murky, skip the swim and simply rest on the rocks instead.
The moss-covered boulders, the fern-lined forest, and the falls behind them make for striking wide-angle shots. Sunlight reaches into the canyon around
10 AM to 1 PM
, when the light is brightest; on overcast days, the water shows up softer in photos.

The road climbing from Dumaguete up to Valencia gains altitude gradually, and the air cools as you go. Riding by motorbike or rental car lets you enjoy views of Mount Talinis and the sea off Dumaguete along the way.

blocks.title: Pulangbato Falls and Red Rock Hot Spring

children.text: Also in Valencia, Pulangbato Falls is known for water running between red-tinted rocks, and the nearby Red Rock hot spring lets you soak in warm sulfur water. It's about
20–30 minutes
from Casaroro by car, so the two pair well together.

Going to Casaroro early in the morning means fewer people and less heat on the climb. If you want to add Twin Lakes (Balinsasayao), it lies in a different direction and adds considerable travel time, so a full-day vehicle charter is the more efficient choice.
A direct flight from Manila to Sibulan Airport (Dumaguete Airport, DGT) takes about
1 hour 20 minutes to 1 hour 30 minutes
. Cebu also has small-plane routes, but schedules change often, so check the latest before you go.
The airport sits in Sibulan, north of downtown Dumaguete, so it's about
30–40 minutes
by car from the airport to Valencia. Most visitors leave their bags at a Dumaguete hotel first and head to the falls the next day.

Take a Ceres bus from Cebu City's south bus terminal to Liloan (Santander) port at the southern tip of Cebu Island, then cross the strait by ferry, landing at Sibulan port on the Negros side. Some through-tickets include the ferry fare. The whole trip to Dumaguete takes about
5–7 hours
, with fares around
Fast ferries also run directly from Cebu port to Dumaguete. Many routes stop at Tagbilaran, Bohol, taking about
4–5 hours
; operators and schedules change often, so confirm before booking.
As of
September 2026
, the Cebu–Dumaguete fast boat is operated by OceanJet, once a day via Tagbilaran, Bohol. It leaves Cebu around

20–30 minutes
, with a fare of about
Around the plaza in Valencia town, bargain with a habal-habal driver to reach the Casaroro entrance. A round trip with waiting time while you visit the falls runs about
(for 1–2 people) — agree on the wait time and fare before you set off.
A half-day tricycle or car charter from Dumaguete costs about
. For groups, chartering a vehicle is convenient and makes it easy to combine with Pulangbato Falls and Red Rock hot spring.
Renting a scooter to drive yourself costs about
per day. The final stretch is steep and slick when wet, so only attempt it if you're confident on a bike.
The eastern coast of Negros Oriental is relatively dry from
December to May
, when the canyon's water level drops, making the stream easier to cross and the falls' pool clearer.
February to April
in particular sees little rain, keeping the trail dry and good for swimming. In
April and May
, though, lowland coastal temperatures climb to
, so an early-morning visit is best. Being in the highlands, Valencia stays a few degrees cooler than Dumaguete.
June to November
is the rainy season, with frequent afternoon showers, and passing typhoons can cause the stream to swell suddenly.
October to December

in particular sees typhoons cross Negros at times, sometimes cutting the trail or forcing temporary closures. If visiting in the rainy season, check the rain forecast for the day before and of your trip, and avoid the day after heavy rain. After rain the falls run thicker and more powerful, but the water turns murky and crossing the stream becomes more dangerous.

There is almost no lodging near Casaroro, so most travelers stay in downtown Dumaguete and visit as a day trip. Dumaguete offers plenty of options, from guesthouses at about
a night to mid-range hotels around Rizal Boulevard at
. For quieter mountain air, you can also stay at a resort or homestay in the Valencia highlands (about
a night) and take your time exploring the falls and hot spring.

At the falls entrance there's a small restaurant serving simple meals and drinks, a good place to rest before or after the trek — but its hours aren't always reliable, so bring water and snacks of your own. Back in Dumaguete, be sure to try the city's signature desserts: sans rival and San Nicolas cookies, layered with meringue and buttercream, are Dumaguete's calling cards, while budbud (glutinous rice steamed in banana leaves) and the thick cocoa drink sikwate are old local breakfast favorites. Restaurants around Rizal Boulevard serve plenty of affordable seafood and barbecue.
The climb back up is the hardest part. Save your energy on the way down, and pace yourself with two or three rest stops on the way up.
Since you'll be crossing streams, aqua shoes or trekking sandals that cover your toes are better than open sandals. Keep your phone and camera in a waterproof pouch.
The trail is clear enough to hike without a guide, but during the rainy season or when the path has been damaged, it's safer to hire a local guide at the entrance.
Ask at the entrance ticket booth about the day's trail conditions and water level. If a bridge is out or the water is high, you may not be able to reach the falls.
Fix the habal-habal fare, including the round trip and waiting time, before you set off, and pay only after you're back.
Bring plenty of water — you'll sweat a lot climbing the stairs, and there's nowhere to buy any inside the canyon.
Go on a quiet weekday morning and you can nearly have the falls to yourself. Local families tend to visit more on weekend and holiday afternoons.
If you have a spare day, Dumaguete travel agencies can book a Valencia tour covering Pulangbato Falls and Red Rock hot spring in one trip.
By executive order in
October 2025
, the town of Valencia closed the Mount Talinis (Cuernos de Negros) trails within the town temporarily and indefinitely. Casaroro Falls itself is operating normally according to
visitor reviews, but the Talinis summit and the traverse course over the mountain from Apolong are not accessible, so check the latest notices at the Valencia tourism office or the entrance.
Admission is paid in cash at the restaurant-cum-ticket booth at the stairs entrance. Foreigners are often quoted a guide fee of about
first, but the path is clear and you can manage in the dry season without a guide, so negotiate and use one only when you need it.

After heavy rain or right after a typhoon, the stream can rise suddenly, making the crossing very dangerous. Postpone your visit if heavy rain is forecast, and always follow the site caretaker's instructions if access is blocked.
The steps and rocks are very slippery with moss. Hold the railing as you walk, and don't run or climb recklessly onto wet rocks for photos.
Right beneath the falls, the current and the force of the falling water are strong and the water is cold. If you're not a confident swimmer, stay in the shallow edges only, and never go in alone.
Small stones can fall from above the falls, so don't linger directly beneath the rock wall.
Phone signal is weak inside the canyon and rescue personnel aren't nearby. If you have weak knees or a heart condition, don't push yourself on the round-trip climb.
Take all your trash out with you, and don't use shampoo or soap in the falls pool — this water is also used by the village downstream.
